subject: Economy
sub_topic: Demand and supply — shifts and determinants

concepts.name: Law of Demand: Exceptions and Limitations
key_dimensions: Giffen goods vs. inferior goods — the critical distinction UPSC exploits
Veblen goods (conspicuous consumption) and the upward-sloping demand curve
Speculative demand (e.g., real estate, gold) where rising price increases demand
Emergency/necessity goods where price elasticity is near-zero (medicines, insulin)

concepts.name: Movement Along vs. Shift of the Demand Curve
key_dimensions: Extension/contraction of demand (movement) caused ONLY by price change
Increase/decrease in demand (shift) caused by non-price determinants
UPSC trap: Identifying whether a scenario causes movement or shift
Graphical implication: same curve vs. new curve — a frequent MCQ anchor

concepts.name: Determinants of Demand: Income Effect and Types of Goods
key_dimensions: Normal goods: positive income effect — demand rises with income
Inferior goods: negative income effect — demand falls as income rises
Giffen goods as a special subset of inferior goods with perverse price effect
UPSC trap: All Giffen goods are inferior but NOT all inferior goods are Giffen

concepts.name: Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand: Substitutes and Complements
key_dimensions: Positive cross-price elasticity → substitute goods (e.g., tea and coffee)
Negative cross-price elasticity → complementary goods (e.g., car and petrol)
Zero cross-price elasticity → unrelated/independent goods
Policy application: taxing one good to reduce demand for its substitute/complement

concepts.name: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED): Determinants and Policy Implications
key_dimensions: Key determinants: availability of substitutes, necessity vs. luxury, proportion of income, time horizon
Perfectly inelastic demand and its relevance to essential commodities/drug pricing
Relationship between PED and total revenue (TR) — a classic UPSC calculation trap
Government taxation strategy: why inelastic goods (tobacco, petrol) are preferred tax targets

concepts.name: Income Elasticity of Demand (YED) and Engel's Law
key_dimensions: Engel's Law: as income rises, proportion spent on food falls — basis of poverty measurement
YED > 1 → luxury goods; 0 < YED < 1 → necessities; YED < 0 → inferior goods
Application to structural change in economy: shift from agriculture to services with rising income
UPSC trap: distinguishing between income elasticity determining good type vs. price elasticity

concepts.name: Shifts in Demand: Role of Consumer Expectations
key_dimensions: Expected future price rise → current demand increases (rightward shift) — speculative buying
Expected income change affecting current consumption decisions
Relevance to inflation psychology and its self-fulfilling nature
RBI/monetary policy linkage: managing inflationary expectations to stabilize demand

concepts.name: Shifts in Demand: Tastes, Preferences, and Advertising
key_dimensions: Autonomous vs. induced changes in taste (social trends vs. advertising)
Demographic shifts as structural demand shifters (e.g., ageing population → healthcare demand)
Seasonal demand shifts vs. permanent preference shifts — policy relevance
UPSC application: demand for organic food, EVs — linking preference shifts to government nudges

concepts.name: Law of Supply and Its Exceptions
key_dimensions: Backward-bending supply curve of labour — when higher wages reduce labour supply
Agricultural supply exceptions: distress selling — farmers sell MORE at lower prices
Speculative supply withholding: traders restrict supply when prices are expected to rise
UPSC trap: Supply of antiques/land — perfectly inelastic (fixed supply) regardless of price

concepts.name: Movement Along vs. Shift of the Supply Curve
key_dimensions: Extension/contraction of supply caused ONLY by change in own price
Increase/decrease in supply caused by non-price factors (technology, input costs, taxes)
UPSC trap: A subsidy to producers shifts supply curve RIGHT — frequently confused with price change
Distinction between supply and quantity supplied in policy-oriented questions

concepts.name: Determinants of Supply: Input Costs and Technology
key_dimensions: Rise in input/factor costs → leftward shift of supply (supply decreases)
Technological improvement → rightward shift of supply (more at same price)
MSP (Minimum Support Price) and its effect on agricultural supply decisions
Supply-side economics: tax cuts and deregulation as supply shifters — Laffer Curve linkage

concepts.name: Price Elasticity of Supply (PES): Determinants and Time Horizons
key_dimensions: Key determinants: time period (momentary/short-run/long-run), spare capacity, storability, factor mobility
Perfectly inelastic supply in ultra-short period (market period) — e.g., fish at market
Long-run supply more elastic than short-run: Marshall's time-period analysis
Policy implication: why supply-side reforms take time — infrastructure investment lag

concepts.name: Market Equilibrium: Price and Quantity Determination
key_dimensions: Equilibrium as intersection of demand and supply — neither surplus nor shortage
Disequilibrium: excess demand (shortage) causes price to rise; excess supply (surplus) causes price to fall
Stable vs. unstable equilibrium — Walrasian vs. Marshallian stability conditions
UPSC application: how MSP creates surplus in grain markets; how rent control creates housing shortage

concepts.name: Simultaneous Shifts in Demand and Supply: Indeterminate Outcomes
key_dimensions: When both curves shift in same direction: price indeterminate, quantity change determinable
When both curves shift in opposite directions: quantity indeterminate, price change determinable
UPSC trap: Questions that give both a supply shock and demand change — test of which dominates
Real-world application: COVID-19 impact on various markets — supply disruption + demand collapse

concepts.name: Price Ceiling (Maximum Price) and Its Economic Consequences
key_dimensions: Set BELOW equilibrium price to make goods affordable — creates excess demand/shortage
Black markets, rationing, and quality deterioration as unintended consequences
Indian examples: Essential Commodities Act, rent control, drug price caps (NPPA/DPCO)
UPSC trap: Price ceiling set ABOVE equilibrium has no effect — a common MCQ trick

concepts.name: Price Floor (Minimum Price) and Its Economic Consequences
key_dimensions: Set ABOVE equilibrium price to protect producers — creates excess supply/surplus
MSP as a price floor in Indian agricultural markets and its fiscal implications for FCI
Minimum wage as a price floor in labour market — debates on employment effect
UPSC trap: Price floor set BELOW equilibrium has no effect — mirror trap to price ceiling question

concepts.name: Producer Surplus and Consumer Surplus: Welfare Analysis
key_dimensions: Consumer surplus: difference between willingness to pay and actual price paid
Producer surplus: difference between actual price received and minimum acceptable price
Deadweight loss from price controls, taxes, or monopoly — welfare triangle concept
Policy application: how subsidies and taxes redistribute surplus between consumers and producers

concepts.name: Elasticity and Tax Incidence: Who Bears the Burden?
key_dimensions: Tax burden falls MORE on the inelastic side (buyer or seller) — the core UPSC rule
If demand is perfectly inelastic: entire tax burden on consumer; if perfectly elastic: entirely on producer
GST and indirect tax incidence — relevance to regressive vs. progressive taxation debate
UPSC trap: Legal incidence (who pays tax to government) vs. economic incidence (who actually bears burden)

concepts.name: Demand for Public Goods vs. Private Goods: Market Failure Link
key_dimensions: Public goods: non-rival and non-excludable → free-rider problem → demand cannot be revealed in market
Market fails to provide public goods optimally — justification for government provision
Quasi-public goods (toll roads, cable TV) — partial excludability, policy relevance
UPSC application: defence, street lighting as pure public goods; vaccination with positive externality

concepts.name: Network Effects and Demand Externalities
key_dimensions: Positive network externality: demand increases as more users adopt (e.g., WhatsApp, UPI)
Bandwagon effect: consumers buy because others buy — reinforces demand shifts
Snob effect: consumers avoid goods that become mass-market — reduces demand with popularity
UPSC application: India's digital payment ecosystem growth — network effects in policy context
